using-imports-and-helper-files.label: Using Imports and Helper Files
using-imports-and-helper-files.summary: Move reusable functions into sibling Python module files, import those functions into `main.py`, and connect multiple focused modules without changing the program's behavior.

sc-file-to-module.title: Import from a sibling file
sc-file-to-module.prompt: `names.py` is beside `main.py` and defines `clean_name`. Which line imports that function into `main.py`?
sc-file-to-module.hint: Use the Python file name without the `.py` extension.

help.concept: A sibling file such as `names.py` can be imported by its module name `names`.
help.hint_2: A direct function import uses `from names import clean_name`.

sc-direct-call.title: Call a directly imported function
sc-direct-call.prompt: After `from names import clean_name`, which expression calls the imported function with `raw_name`?
sc-direct-call.hint: A directly imported function is called by its function name.

help.concept: With `from module import function`, the imported function name is available directly in the importing file.
help.hint_1: You do not include `.py` when calling the function.

sc-module-responsibility.title: Choose a focused helper module
sc-module-responsibility.prompt: Which file responsibility is the clearest fit for a small helper module?

help.concept: A helper module is easiest to understand when its functions serve one related responsibility.
help.hint_1: Name-related cleanup functions belong naturally together.
help.hint_2: Avoid a file that mixes unrelated input, math, formatting, and random experiments.

options.a: `names.py` contains functions for cleaning and formatting names
options.b: `everything.py` contains unrelated code from the entire program
options.c: `main.py` copies every helper function before using it

sc-main-role.title: What main.py should do
sc-main-role.prompt: After name cleanup lives in `names.py` and badge formatting lives in `badges.py`, what is a good responsibility for `main.py`?
sc-main-role.hint: The main file can coordinate the app instead of duplicating helper logic.

help.concept: `main.py` can read input, call imported helpers, and connect their returned values into the program flow.
help.hint_1: The helper modules already own cleanup and badge formatting.
help.hint_2: The main file should import and call them rather than rewrite them.

options.a: Read input and connect the imported helper functions
options.b: Copy the full contents of every helper file
options.c: Rename every imported function before it can run

sibling-module.title: A Python file can be imported as a module
sibling-module.bodyMarkdown:
A helper function does not have to stay in `main.py`. A sibling Python file can hold that function instead.

Suppose these two files sit beside each other:

```text
main.py
names.py
```

`names.py` can contain:

```python
def display_name(text):
    return text.strip().title()
```

Then `main.py` can import that function:

```python
from names import display_name

raw = input()
print(display_name(raw))
```

The file `names.py` becomes the module named `names`. The import uses the module name without `.py`: `from names import display_name`.

For this lesson, helper modules live beside `main.py`; no package folders are needed.

related-helpers.title: One module can hold related helpers
related-helpers.bodyMarkdown:
A module can contain more than one function when those functions share a clear responsibility.

For example, `text_tools.py` might contain two text-formatting helpers:

```python
def clean_text(text):
    return text.strip().lower()

def emphasize(text):
    return text.upper() + "!"
```

`main.py` can import both names directly:

```python
from text_tools import clean_text, emphasize

text = clean_text("  Hello  ")
print(emphasize(text))
```

The module name is `text_tools`; `clean_text` and `emphasize` are function names defined inside that module.

connect-modules.title: main.py can connect multiple helper modules
connect-modules.bodyMarkdown:
As a program grows, different helper files can own different jobs while `main.py` connects them.

```text
main.py
names.py
labels.py
```

`main.py` can import from both modules:

```python
from names import display_name
from labels import make_label

name = display_name("  mia  ")
print(make_label(name))
```

Here `names.py` owns name cleanup, `labels.py` owns label formatting, and `main.py` owns the application flow that passes one returned value into the next helper.

This keeps each responsibility in one place without introducing package folders or advanced import patterns.
